title: Reading one line of his
hook: pick one line of the Tenth Guru and live with it for a day

segments.voice: Yesterday, sword and pen: the saint-soldier, with doing good written before the sword. Your line was pen and sword.

A tune heard once at breakfast can still be playing in your head at dinner. Nobody learned it on purpose. It was short enough to stay, and by evening it had been everywhere you went. Sikh life has a version of this. In a gurdwara, the morning's hukamnama, one hymn read from the Guru Granth Sahib, is carried home by some Sikhs as the word for the day. Today, try that with the Tenth Guru. Not his whole book. One line.
screen: `A TUNE THAT STAYS ALL DAY.` → `THE WORD FOR THE DAY.` → `NOT THE WHOLE BOOK. ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: Here are three lines from his writings, met along the way, each paraphrased. The first is from the Akal Ustat: recognize the whole human race as one. That's a line for a crowded train, for the person you'd rather not sit next to. Live with it for a day and every face becomes a test of it. The second comes from the morning swayyas, which sit in the same work. The Guru says: I tell you the truth, all of you, listen: only those who have loved have found the Lord. That's a line about the heart under the ritual. Live with it and you start asking where love actually went in what you did. The third is from the Bachitar Natak, about himself. Whoever calls me God, he warns, will fall; I am only the servant of the Supreme. A line about humility, from someone with every reason to be proud. Live with it and watch how often you'd like a little credit. Why only one? Because a line has to be carried to be read. Read a whole page and it stays on the page. Carry one line and it starts reading you back, at the sink, in a meeting, in a mood. That fits a habit in Sikh life: the word isn't finished when the book closes. One line, one day, is enough to find out what the Tenth Guru's words do when they leave the page.
screen: `ONE HUMAN RACE: A LINE FOR CROWDS.` · `ONLY THOSE WHO LOVED FOUND THE LORD.` · `ONLY THE SERVANT: A LINE FOR PRIDE.` · `CARRY ONE, AND IT READS YOU BACK.` · then, large: `ONE LINE, ONE DAY.`

segments.voice: Let the three pass by again, one human race, only those who loved, only the servant, and choose the one that pricks a little, not the one you think is best. Say it slowly in your head, half on the in-breath, half on the out, and if you pray, let it rest beside the name Waheguru.
Reading one line of his. Choosing a single line of Guru Gobind Singh's writings and carrying it through a whole day, so the words leave the page. Today's word.
screen: `READING ONE LINE OF HIS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: one line, one day. Three lines offered, and one is enough. Twelve hundred fifty days now.

screen: `DAY 1250 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TENTH GURU'S WRITINGS CLOSE.`

howItsDone: Some Sikhs carry the morning hukamnama from the gurdwara as the word for the day, and some take a line from the Nitnem, including the Tenth Guru's compositions, to recall through the day.

chat.says: Why carry just one line from the Tenth Guru's writings? Why not read a whole page?
options: A page stays on the page; one line carried through the day starts reading you back.
Because his writings are too hard to understand beyond a single line.
Because Sikhs are only allowed to read one line of his each day.
chat.meaning: A line has to be carried to be read. Carried all day, it shows up at the sink, in a meeting, in a mood.

Akal Ustat.meaning: the Tenth Guru's hymn in praise of the Timeless One

swayyas.meaning: short verses; here, the morning set in the same work

Bachitar Natak.meaning: a verse life story in the Dasam Granth, in the Tenth Guru's voice

hukamnama.meaning: a hymn read from the opened Granth as the day's word

sources.ref: Akal Ustat 85 (Dasam Granth): recognize all humankind as one, paraphrased
Tav Prasad Swayye (Akal Ustat): only those who have loved have found the Lord, paraphrased
Bachitar Natak 6 (Dasam Granth): whoever calls me God will fall; I am the servant, paraphrased

notes: All three lines are paraphrased; please check the paraphrases and the references (Akal Ustat 85; 'sach kahon sun leho sabhai, jin prem kio tin hi prabh paio' in the Tav Prasad Swayye; Bachitar Natak 6).
The Bachitar Natak line says those who call him God will fall into hell; the script softens it to 'will fall'. Please confirm this is acceptable.
'Some Sikhs carry the morning hukamnama home as the word for the day' is a general description; please confirm or soften.
